title: An Execution‑Oriented Evaluation of Generate→Validate→Simulate→Rollback Pipelines for LLM‑Assisted NetOps: a Confirmatory Study with gpt‑5‑mini
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory comparison of (A) a generation‑only pipeline and (C) a generate→validate→simulate→rollback (guarded) pipeline for LLM‑assisted NetOps configuration tasks (preregistration id: c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1). Under the frozen plan we ran gpt‑5‑mini on N=160 vendor‑neutral tasks (routing/ACL/NAT). A deterministic simulator adjudicated an actionable‑misconfiguration binary per task. Results (artifact‑backed): baseline actionable = 0/160; guarded actionable = 0/160; paired difference = 0.00; bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) [0.00,0.00]; McNemar exact p = 1.00. The preregistered target (≥30% relative reduction) is not evaluable because the baseline actionable rate was zero (ceiling effect). We (1) archive full preregistration, provider call logs, per‑task scoring JSONs, and analysis artifacts (SHA‑256 hashes recorded in the execution manifest), (2) describe the simulator‑scoring linkage and execution semantics, and (3) discuss construct/externally‑valid limitations and concrete recommendations for harder confirmatory sets and multi‑model follow‑ups.

sections.introduction: Motivation and gap. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks (intent→configuration, change planning, limited self‑healing), but fluent proposals can be operationally risky if enacted without deterministic pre‑enactment assurance [VeriFlow 2012; MeshAgent 2025]. Prior works pair generation and verification, yet transparent, preregistered, execution‑oriented comparisons that tie generation to deterministic enactment outcomes are rare. Research question. Under a frozen preregistered plan (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1), does a generate→validate→simulate→rollback (guarded) pipeline (C) reduce the actionable‑misconfiguration rate by ≥30% relative to a generation‑only baseline (A) on a representative vendor‑neutral NetOps task set? Contributions. We present (i) a fully preregistered paired confirmatory execution using gpt‑5‑mini with artifacted inputs/outputs and SHA‑256 integrity; (ii) deterministic simulator adjudication and archived per‑task scoring; (iii) honest reporting of a ceiling effect and prescriptive recommendations for future, harder confirmatory designs.
sections.related_work: Verification and guarded generation. VeriFlow introduced dynamic invariant checking at rule insertion time to prevent emergent policy violations [Khurshid et al., Sigcomm 2012]. More recent NetOps work pairs LLM generation with constraint validation or verifiers (e.g., Verified Prompt Programming, MeshAgent, GraphSynth/MNC family) to reduce syntactic/semantic errors. Ops/AIOps benchmarks (OpsEval, LogEval families) stress task realism but typically focus on QA/accuracy rather than deterministic enactability. Our study differs by preregistration, artifacted end‑to‑end enactment scoring, and paired statistical design linking generation to an operationally framed simulator predicate.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen design. The full preregistration (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1) froze task selection, augmentation seeds [42,123,999], model scope (gpt‑5‑mini), paired confirmatory design (N=160 tasks), primary estimand, analysis plan, retry policy, and stopping rules. Task set. Confirmatory N=160 vendor‑neutral tasks were sampled per the preregistered script and augmented deterministically: routing ≈64, ACL ≈64, NAT/other ≈32 (selection scripts and input hashes are archived). Model calling semantics and shared generation. The run used a single shared initial generation per task that was used for both conditions (baseline and guarded); provider_call_audit in the execution manifest records stage_counts: {"shared_initial_generation":160} (see execution manifest and provider_call_audit entries). This pre‑registered choice preserved a strict paired comparison on the same candidate per task rather than independent per‑condition generations. Guarded pipeline. For each shared candidate the guarded pipeline canonicalized the output, applied a constraint/validator stage, ran the deterministic simulator to adjudicate actionability, and, when allowed, recorded rollback decisions per the frozen scoring schema. Baseline pipeline. The generation‑only baseline produced the same shared candidate; the simulator scored the candidate post‑hoc but the baseline did not block enactment. Outcome and analysis. Primary outcome: binary actionable misconfiguration per task as returned by the deterministic simulator. Pre‑registered primary analysis: paired bootstrap (10,000 replicates, seed=1729) for CI and McNemar exact test for paired binary outcome. Reproducibility. All prompts, seeds, canonicalizers, raw outputs (execution/responses/*), per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json), and provider call logs (execution/provider_calls/*.json) are archived with SHA‑256 hashes in the execution manifest (representative hashes cited in Results).
sections.results: Execution and main verified facts (artifact references and hashes recorded in the execution manifest). Execution completed per preregistration: planned maximum model calls = 320; actual model calls used = 160 because one shared initial generation was used per task (execution manifest: provider_call_audit and model_call accounting). Confirmatory paired outcomes: complete pairs = 160. Observed actionable counts: baseline actionable = 0/160; guarded actionable = 0/160. Contingency: n11 (non‑actionable both) = 160; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. Paired difference (baseline minus guarded) = 0.00. Bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729): [0.00,0.00]. McNemar exact two‑sided p = 1.00. Clustered descriptive counts (preregistered cluster sizes and observed actionable counts). Per the frozen sampling plan: routing tasks = 64 (actionable=0), ACL tasks = 64 (actionable=0), NAT/other tasks = 32 (actionable=0). Validator blocking, repairs, and false‑positive rate (artifact‑derived). From the archived scoring manifests and provider call logs: blocked_by_validator = 0; repairs_attempted = 0; repairs_accepted_and_rescored = 0. By the preregistered definition (validator false‑positive = fraction of tasks where the validator blocked a configuration that the simulator would not flag actionable), observed validator false‑positive rate = 0/160 = 0. Representative artifact pointers (files and SHA‑256 hashes appear in the execution manifest): execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: 2445d0f8e9be9cfa34ede1bbe80b82d6f05b51bcafc7c1688d0ed8e1c73d8044), execution/result_schema.json (SHA‑256: 63199db3f7219b969acc5497fae613c8d5df16e081768969f67b7b3024844465), execution/transformation_manifest.json (SHA‑256: 28c190a50d06bf19894639f0ed6edc7b2dc3771138bd818422c212c316bf7c5c), execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (SHA‑256: 9730d4b08759b4771b5742a7789edf9ff1fc2ed4e8ee69bdc5c783720a2d2ab8). Example end‑to‑end chain (artifact references only). For task task-000001 the archived artifacts include: generation text (execution/responses/task-000001-baseline.txt; SHA‑256 recorded), guarded scoring JSON (execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json; SHA‑256 recorded). The manifest contains full per‑file hashes for inspection and independent re‑scoring.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and ceiling effect. The preregistered power plan assumed a nonzero baseline actionable rate (conservative design used baseline p≈0.30). Observing baseline=0 produces a ceiling effect that makes the preregistered ≥30% relative‑reduction target unevaluable. The observed degenerate result is artifact‑backed and arises from the joint effect of (i) task calibration (the sampled vendor‑neutral tasks produced candidates judged non‑actionable by the simulator) and (ii) the single shared‑candidate design: because one shared initial candidate was used per task, if that candidate is already non‑actionable the guarded pipeline cannot demonstrate a reduction for that task. Construct validity. Our primary estimand is reduction in 'actionable misconfigurations' as defined by the deterministic simulator predicate archived in execution/result_schema.json and per‑task scoring JSONs; the external validity of conclusions depends on how well that predicate aligns with an operator's safety requirements. Recommendations for future confirmatory runs. (1) Calibrate tasks to produce a nonzero baseline actionable rate (use adversarial/harder discovery items or broaden predicate scope). (2) Evaluate multiple models and prompt strategies rather than a single shared generation per task to allow the guarded pipeline to block or repair diverse erroneous candidates. (3) Broaden simulator predicates and optionally include human adjudication for higher‑fidelity operational outcomes. Reproducibility and artifacted transparency. All inputs, outputs, provider call logs, and analysis scripts are archived; representative hashes are listed above and the full manifest contains exhaustive per‑file hashes for independent verification (see execution manifest).
sections.conclusion: We carried out a fully preregistered, artifacted, paired confirmatory comparison of a generation‑only pipeline and a generate→validate→simulate→rollback guarded pipeline for LLM‑assisted NetOps using gpt‑5‑mini on 160 vendor‑neutral tasks. Observed outcome: baseline actionable=0/160 and guarded actionable=0/160 (paired difference 0.00; 95% CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p=1.00). Because baseline was zero, the preregistered ≥30% relative‑reduction target is unevaluable. The run is transparently archived (full per‑file SHA‑256 hashes in the execution manifest) and highlights that demonstrable operational benefits of guarded pipelines require (i) tasks that yield nonzero baseline enactable faults, (ii) multi‑model/prompt scope, and (iii) richer scoring predicates or human adjudication. We publish the artifacts and recommend calibrated follow‑on confirmatory runs per the directions above.

disclosure_statement:
Mandatory Disclosure Statement (CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track).

Models, adapter, and orchestration: primary generative model = gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API). Orchestration and execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family under the frozen preregistration c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1. The exact initial master prompt bundle (Master Prompt v1 — Autonomous CNSM 2026 Research Run) and the autonomy boundary are recorded in the preregistration and manifest. Topic constraints: the Research Director selected the broad family “Generative AI and Large Language Models for NetOps” and constrained the scope to operational reliability, validation, and enactability; those constraints are recorded in the preregistration.

Pre‑lock development and autonomy boundary: collaborative pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred and were explicitly excluded from final empirical evidence as required by the track. After the autonomy lock, literature search, research‑gap selection, preregistration, prompt generation, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, autonomous peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting were performed autonomously. No human manually edited technical manuscript content, numerical results, figures, captions, references, or this Disclosure Statement after the autonomy lock.

Preregistration and frozen design: full experimental plan preregistered as c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1 and frozen before execution. Key preregistered elements included: task selection, augmentation seeds, model scope (gpt‑5‑mini), maximum model calls (320), paired confirmatory design (N=160 tasks), primary metric (actionable misconfiguration binary), analysis plan (paired bootstrap 10k, McNemar exact), retry policy, and stopping rules. No post‑hoc changes affecting confirmatory analysis occurred.

Execution artifacts and integrity: all experiment artifacts (preregistration, raw model outputs, provider call logs, canonicalized configurations, per‑task scoring JSONs, deterministic simulator scoring schema, and analysis scripts) are archived. Representative artifact references and SHA‑256 hashes (recorded in the execution manifest) include execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: 2445d0f8e9be9cfa34ede1bbe80b82d6f05b51bcafc7c1688d0ed8e1c73d8044), execution/result_schema.json (SHA‑256: 63199db3f7219b969acc5497fae613c8d5df16e081768969f67b7b3024844465), execution/transformation_manifest.json (SHA‑256: 28c190a50d06bf19894639f0ed6edc7b2dc3771138bd818422c212c316bf7c5c), and the per‑task scoring JSONs under execution/scoring/ (full listing and hashes appear in the execution manifest). These artifacts are the canonical integrity‑verified record for replication and re‑scoring. No invented URLs or repository locations are claimed here beyond the manifest artifact paths and hashes.

Model calls and retries: preregistered maximum model calls = 320; actual model calls used = 160 (one shared initial generation per task). Provider call logs and the call cache are archived; provider_call_audit in the deterministic reconciliation shows stage_counts: {"shared_initial_generation":160} and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed=false. Retries were pre‑registered (up to two) for transient provider failures; none affected confirmatory outcomes.

Human role and limitations: the human Research Director selected the topic family and approved pre‑lock infrastructure development; post‑lock scientific execution and manuscript drafting were autonomous. Precise provider endpoint identifiers and internal provider operational logs are not published here for confidentiality; everything required to reproduce the analysis given the same hosted model API (prompts, seeds, canonicalizers, simulator scoring schema, raw outputs, and per‑artifact SHA‑256) is archived and referenced in the execution manifest. The manifest and artifact SHA‑256 hashes are authoritative for verification of the run.
limitations: Ceiling effect: baseline generation produced zero actionable misconfigurations under the chosen deterministic simulator (baseline=0/160), making the preregistered ≥30% relative‑reduction target unevaluable.
Single‑model scope: results apply to gpt‑5‑mini and the supplied prompts/call budget only; multi‑model generalization is unresolved.

Construct coverage: the deterministic simulator scoring predicate is an abstraction; it may not capture all operational failure modes—inspect execution/result_schema.json and execution/scoring/*.json (SHA‑256 hashes in the execution manifest) to verify predicate details.
Task calibration: confirmatory task set difficulty did not produce a nonzero baseline actionable rate; future confirmatory runs must use adversarial/harder tasks or broaden predicate scope.
No live device enactment: evaluation used deterministic simulator adjudication rather than live production enactment; external validity to production remains limited.
